stops.name: Marienthal, the duke's gift: the last garden
stops.campa: Won by Marenholtz-Bülow's advocacy, Duke Georg of Saxe-Meiningen gives Fröbel the little hunting-château of Marienthal, between Liebenstein and Schweina, for his training institution. The old man moves in with his kindergartners-in-training, his Gifts, his songs; the meadows become playgrounds, the château a mother-school. Twenty years after Helba fell through, a Meiningen duke at last houses the idea, not the grand national institute of 1829, but its ripened seed: a house where young women learn the tending of childhood. Marienthal, Mary's valley, the gardener's last garden.

stops.name: Marienthal, marriage to Louise Levin
stops.campa: On 9 June 1851 the sixty-nine-year-old Fröbel marries Louise Levin, thirty-six, once a housekeeping pupil at Keilhau, long the most devoted worker of the household. The tongues of the neighbourhood and even of old friends wag; the marriage answers them by simply being what it is: the ordering of the last workshop. Louise stands beside him through the year of the ban, keeps the house of the training school, and after his death will carry his papers, his letters and his cause for half a century of widowhood. The last brotherhood he founds has one member.

stops.name: Marienthal, the Prussian Kindergarten Ban
stops.campa: On 7 August 1851 the Prussian minister von Raumer outlaws the kindergarten throughout Prussia as 'atheistic and demagogic', destructive in religion and politics: the minister has confounded Friedrich with his socialist nephew Karl, whose book on women's colleges and kindergartens frightened the reaction. Varnhagen writes it plainly in his diary: the stupid minister has confused the two Fröbels. The error is exposed; Raumer, rather than admit it, lets the ban stand. The old man at Marienthal, who fought Napoleon for the children of Prussia, sees Prussia close its gardens against the children. The grief never quite leaves him; the ban outlives him by eight years.

stops.name: Marienthal, the seventieth birthday festival
stops.campa: On 21 April 1852 the banned man turns seventy, and Marienthal answers Berlin with flowers. Kindergartners, Keilhau brothers, children of the villages come with garlands and ring-games; the meadows fill with song; the old man is crowned by the small hands his life has served. Middendorff speaks; the children dance the circle-games from the Mutter- und Koselieder around their gardener. Those present remember it afterwards as a transfiguration, the whole doctrine visible for one afternoon: the unity of life, celebrated by playing children in a garden, with the state's prohibition powerless at the fence.

stops.name: Gotha, the teachers rise to greet him
stops.campa: Weeks before the end, Fröbel travels to the general congress of German teachers at Gotha. When the white-haired man enters, the great assembly rises to greet him as one body. The profession that ignored, mocked and suspected him for forty years stands up for the banned founder of the garden of children. Honour arrives, as it likes to, at the door of death. He receives the ovation gently and speaks of the work, not the wound. It is his last journey. He returns to Marienthal carrying the teachers' homage like late fruit, out of season and sweet.

stops.name: Marienthal, death of the gardener
stops.campa: Midsummer 1852: fifty-five years to the season since the boy was bound to the forester on Midsummer Day. On 21 June, at Marienthal, with Louise and the faithful about him and the windows open to the green he loved, Friedrich Fröbel dies. He goes out at the year's greatest light, asking that his flowers be tended and grieving nothing but the closed gardens of Prussia. Middendorff, his Aaron, survives him barely a year; the ban survives him eight; the kindergarten survives him everywhere. The unfolding he preached in crystal, plant and child now claims the preacher.

stops.name: Schweina, the grave under the sphere, cylinder and cube
stops.campa: On 24 June 1852 they carry him from Marienthal up to the hillside churchyard of Schweina, children and kindergartners walking in the procession, and lay him in earth within sight of the Thuringian forest that first mothered him. Over the grave the tradition raises his own second Gift monumentally in stone, sphere upon cylinder upon cube, the eternal law of unfolding set as a tombstone, and cuts beneath it the six words of his life. Lilies, his flower, six-petaled like the motto, are planted round. The gardener is himself planted; the gardens keep coming up, in every country, every autumn, ever since.
stops.quote: Kommt, lasst uns unsern Kindern leben!
stops.quote_source: Fröbel's motto (Sonntagsblatt, 1838), inscribed on the gravestone at Schweina
